subject: Maths
central_question: How can an unknown quantity be represented by a letter, translated into an equation and found by preserving equality through inverse operations?
in_scope_units: 7.1 Find the Unknowns—Unknown Weights: interpreting balanced scales and removing equal quantities from both sides.
Matchstick Pattern and Equations: representing the nth pattern with a letter-number and solving conditions such as 2n + 1 = 99.
7.2 Solving Equations Systematically: understanding equations, LHS, RHS, solutions, trial and error and equality-preserving operations.
Inverse Operations and Transposition: removing terms or factors through additive inverses, division and multiplication.
Unknowns on Both Sides: collecting unknown terms on one side and known terms on the other.
Solving Problems: forming equations from tile patterns, savings, parties, math tricks, ages, prices and sharing situations.
Generating Equations: creating multiple equations with a specified solution and interpreting equations in context.
7.3 Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: locating, explaining and correcting errors in equation-solving steps.
7.4 A Pinch of History: bījagaṇita, Brahmagupta, Al-Khwarizmi, ancient symbols for unknowns and Bhāskarāchārya's horse-price problem.
Final Figure it Out: solving Questions 1–20 involving machines, taxi fares, number relations, geometry, equations and heads-and-feet reasoning.
banned_topics: Simultaneous linear equations as a formal elimination or substitution method.

known_pitfalls.claim: A term can simply be moved across the equality sign and its sign changed without explanation.
known_pitfalls.correction: This shorthand represents applying an inverse operation equally so that the balance of the equation is preserved.

known_pitfalls.claim: An operation used on one side of an equation need not be used on the other side.
known_pitfalls.correction: The same equality-preserving operation must be applied to both sides.

known_pitfalls.claim: In 2(x + 1), the factor 2 multiplies only x.
The first value obtained is automatically the solution.
known_pitfalls.correction: Substitute the value into the original equation and verify that LHS equals RHS.

known_pitfalls.claim: A dash or diagram can be translated into any convenient equation.
known_pitfalls.correction: Every number, operation and relationship in the equation must match the stated situation.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every equation has exactly one solution.
known_pitfalls.correction: Some equations may have no solution or may express an equality true for more than one value, although the chapter mainly solves single-solution linear equations.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with the balanced-scale sack activities in Figs. 7.9–7.12 to establish doing the same thing on both sides.
Use the matchstick pattern and equation 2n + 1 = 99 to connect patterns, letter-numbers and equations.
Use 5x − 4 = 7, Example 5 and Example 6 to teach inverse operations and unknowns on both sides.
Use Example 7's tile pattern 3k + 1 and Examples 9–11 on savings, brackets and the math trick for modelling.
Use the Mind the Mistake section on pages 181–182 to diagnose sign and distribution errors.
Use Example 16, Bhāskarāchārya's horse-price problem, to connect history and equation solving.
Conclude with final Figure it Out Questions 1–20 on pages 185–189.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The concluding Figure it Out exercise spans pages 185–189 and contains Questions 1–20, including the equation maze and heads-and-feet problem.
